catalog_quote: A number of tonal contrasts can be observed in Lopit. In the present data, there is evidence for three lexically contrastive tones: High and Low level tones, and a Falling contour tone, which, impressionistically, transitions from high to low pitch targets. The syllable is proposed as the tone-bearing unit, as has been similarly noted by Stirtz (2014b). Table 3.9 provides some examples of tonal contrasts in word-initial, word-medial and word-final positions. ... Some descriptions of Nilotic languages mention word-level stress, or accent, in addition to tone, though likely with reference to a range of perceived phenomena. ... For the Southern and Eastern Nilotic languages, there is little mention of this possibility in later descriptive work, apart from some explicit statements that there is no contrastive stress, for example for Turkana (Heine, 1980, p. 44) and Otuho (Coates, 1985, p. 1…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every segment of the deciding quotation is verbatim in the Billington 2017 text we hold at the stated places (sec. 3.5.1 p.146; sec. 2.4 pp.73-74; ch. 6 conclusion p.330). (2) Deciding source: a 430-page phonetics-and-phonology PhD (2017) with acoustic tone chapters — the Glottolog phonology of record — corroborated by the held Moodie 2019 grammar thesis (three tones H/F/L, lexical and grammatical; no stress/accent mentioned anywhere) and by the Billington 2015 ICPhS paper downloaded now (three tones, syllable TBU, no stress vocabulary). Billington explicitly surveys Nilotic stress claims, notes 'no contrastive stress' statements for the closest relatives (Otuho, Turkana), and posits no stress rule for Lopit, raising metrical prominence only as future work — exactly what the record's the primary-stress rule says.
